title: Production debugging and technical trade-offs
exp: These questions test whether you own production problems or defer them. The strongest answers describe something REAL from your work.
pts: Check data first, then code, then infrastructure. The most common root cause of a 10x slowdown is a data change.
Bug corrupting 2% of records for 3 months: order matters -- stop damage, scope blast radius, communicate, plan backfill.
SQL Server vs Spark: RDBMS for transactional/small/ACID workloads. Spark when data doesn't fit on one machine.
Technical debt: deliberate and documented debt is fine. Silent debt is what compounds into a crisis.

viz.note: Debugging order: data first (volume? skew? type change?) -> code (recent deploy?) -> infrastructure (Spot? OOM?). Never assume infrastructure first.

qa.q: A Spark job that ran fine for 6 months suddenly takes 10x longer. Walk through your investigation.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Check data first: did input volume change? Did a new skewed key appear? Did a source send malformed records causing type coercion? Only after ruling out data: did a recent deploy change the query? In Spark UI: which stage got slow, is one task an outlier (skew), did a new Exchange appear in the plan?

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: You discover a bug corrupting 2% of records for 3 months. What order do you act in?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** (1) Deploy the fix to stop further corruption. (2) Scope the blast radius -- which records, sources, time period, downstream consumers. (3) Communicate proactively before being asked. (4) Plan and execute backfill. Don't do all at once -- stop the bleeding, understand scope, communicate, fix history, in that order.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.
